findings.paper_title: Treasury Managment Annual Report for the Financial Year 25 26
findings.headline: Planned financial restructure of Advance Northumberland did not proceed
findings.detail: The council had budgeted for income to fall following a financial restructure of Advance Northumberland. The restructure did not happen; instead the council received £19.220m from third-party loans—£3.134m above budget. The paper does not explain why the planned restructure was not completed.
findings.matters: Non-completion of a major planned transaction affecting a council-controlled or related entity warrants investigation into whether governance issues or hidden problems in that entity caused the pause
findings.figures: £19.220m actual third-party loan income vs budgeted expectation of ~£16.086m; £3.134m higher than forecast
findings.quote: The budget assumed a reduction in investment income following the proposed financial restructure of Advance Northumberland; however, the restructure did not proceed during 2025-26, resulting in higher income than forecast.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Managment Annual Report for the Financial Year 25 26
findings.headline: Capital programme underspent by £133.66m, a 10.7% shortfall against budget
findings.detail: The capital financing requirement reached £1,109.778m against a budget of £1,243.438m. The council attributes this to 'significant underspends and re-profiling' but provides no detail on which schemes slipped or why. This is a material variance that raises questions about capital delivery capacity.
findings.matters: Substantial capital programme slippage can indicate delivery challenges or reduced investment momentum, which affects how the council will fund future borrowing needs and service debt
findings.figures: £1,109.778m actual CFR vs £1,243.438m budgeted; £133.66m variance (10.7%)
findings.quote: The CFR (excluding PFIs) increased by £52.658 million during the year and was lower than originally budgeted at 31 March 2026 at £1,109.778 million against an original budget of £1,243.438 million. This was due to significant underspends and re-profiling within the 2025-26 capital programme.

findings.headline: Housing regulator found very serious failings and issued lowest-possible C4 rating in February 2026
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing inspection found fundamental changes needed at the Council's housing service. Specific failures include: only 3% of homes have up-to-date condition information, insufficient evidence of health and safety assessments being recorded or monitored, failure to respond to all complaints timely, and serious gaps in tenant scrutiny. The regulator graded the Council as C4 — the lowest possible Consumer Standards grading. The Council has established a Housing Assurance & Compliance Board and stock condition survey (targeting 100% coverage by March 2027), with auditors to review progress.
findings.matters: A lowest-level regulatory rating indicates significant governance and operational failures in a major council service, suggesting broader assurance and management capability issues material to credit risk.
findings.figures: 3% of 8,200 homes have up-to-date condition information; C4 rating (lowest possible grading); stock condition survey to reach 100% coverage by March 2027
findings.quote: As a result of the above findings, the regulator graded the Council as 'C4', which is the lowest grading for the Consumer Standards assessment.

findings.headline: External borrowing increased £63.944m to £898.468m during the year and now stands at 65.18% of Operational Boundary
findings.detail: The council's external borrowing rose from £834.524m to £898.468m, an increase of £63.944m in a single year. The council remains within its Authorised Limit and Operational Boundary, but the direction of travel is material. Borrowing is being used to fund the capital programme, and with capital re-profiling, future years' borrowing requirement will increase.
findings.matters: Rising borrowing levels reduce future flexibility and increase interest rate risk. With capital re-profiling deferred to 2026-27, the council may face higher borrowing needs in the coming year, especially if interest rates remain elevated.
findings.figures: £898.468m total external borrowing (31 March 2026); increase of £63.944m in year; 65.18% of Operational Boundary (from 64.20%)
findings.quote: Total external borrowing has increased by £63.944 million, from £834.524 million at the start of the year to £898.468 million at 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: HRA maintenance pressures from Awaab's Law compliance expected to place "significant financial burden" on housing account in future years
findings.detail: Repairs and Maintenance overspent by £1.259m in 2025-26, with contractor costs up £1.057m. The paper explicitly flags that "damp and mould team following the introduction of Awaab's Law... is expected to place a significant financial burden on the HRA in future years." This is an unfunded statutory liability arising from new regulatory requirements on damp and mould remediation in social housing.
findings.matters: Awaab's Law creates a new, potentially substantial, unfunded liability on the HRA. The council has not quantified the impact, but flags it as material. This is a hidden cost that could force difficult choices in the HRA over the next 2-3 years.
findings.figures: £1.259m overspend in R&M (2025-26); no figure given for Awaab's Law impact
findings.quote: There is an overspend of £0.589 million within Waste Services... Although it is too early to fully quantify the impact of Awaab's Law, it is expected to place a significant financial burden on the HRA in future years.

findings.headline: Capital programme re-profiled £60.971m from 2025-26 to 2026-27, suggesting systematic delivery delays across major projects
findings.detail: The capital programme experienced net re-profiling of £60.971m to the following year, plus an additional £25.864m underspend, for a total variance of £86.835m on a £297.5m final budget. Major reprofiling includes Energising Blyth (£7.977m), Northumberland Line (£7.725m), Highways Maintenance Uplift (£4.313m), and Phase 1 Food Service Rollout (£2.308m). These are not small adjustments but material slippages suggesting either project management issues or demand for capital is lower than planned.
findings.matters: Persistent re-profiling of capital reduces the council's ability to deliver its regeneration and infrastructure agenda. For a lender, it raises questions about project governance and whether schemes represent genuine value for money if they cannot be delivered on schedule.
findings.figures: £60.971m net re-profiling (20% of final budget); £86.835m total variance; Northumberland Line £7.725m; Energising Blyth £7.977m; Phase 1 Food Service £2.308m
findings.quote: The major schemes requiring re-profiling are Energising Blyth Programme (£7.977 million), the Northumberland Line (£7.725 million), Highways Maintenance Uplift Fund (£4.313 million), Phase 1 Food Service Roll Out (£2.308 million) and the Local Transport Plan (£2.039 million).

findings.headline: Children's external residential placements overspent £4.528m, with average weekly placement cost rising from £6,052 to £6,592 and complexity driving additional support needs
findings.detail: The Children, Young People and Families service overspent by £3.857m, with external residential placements accounting for £4.528m of that. The number of placements increased by 6 (to 80 total), but the material driver is cost: average weekly cost per placement rose to £6,592. More significantly, 27% of placements now require additional support packages (up from 16% at year start), reflecting increasing complexity of individual cases.
findings.matters: Rising unit costs and complexity in residential placements, independent of volume growth, signals a shift in the client cohort toward more costly interventions. This is harder to manage through procurement or volume controls.
findings.figures: £4.528m overspend; 80 placements (6 more than prior year); average weekly cost rose to £6,592 (from £6,052); 27% requiring additional support packages (up from 16%)
findings.quote: the average weekly cost of a placement has risen from £6,052 per week in May 2025 to £6,592. In addition, the increasing complexity of individual cases has resulted in 27% of placements requiring additional support packages, up from 16% at the beginning of the financial year.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit reached £20.113m, projected to grow to £48.029m by 2028, with council relying on unconfirmed government support
findings.detail: The High Needs Block overspent by £12.561m in 2025-26, driven by EHCP cohort growth of 21-23% annually and increasing complexity. The cumulative DSG deficit is now £20.113m held in an unusable reserve. Government announced 90% funding via High Needs Stability Grant from 2026-27, but council must fund 10%. Critically, the council states: "There has been no formal announcement for funding between 2026-28 other than it will be proportionate, but not unlimited." The deficit is projected to grow to £48.029m by end of 2028 if in-year overspends continue.
findings.matters: A growing, multi-year deficit in a ring-fenced account that relies on continued government support is a material contingent liability. If government support is withdrawn or inadequate, the council will be forced to find alternative funding or reduce services.
findings.figures: £20.113m cumulative deficit (31 March 2026); projected £48.029m by 31 March 2028; council contribution £2m set aside for 2025-26; government to fund 90% (if confirmed)
findings.quote: There has been no formal announcement for funding between 2026-28 other than it will be proportionate, but not unlimited. Therefore, an assumption has been made that the grant will continue throughout this period.

findings.headline: Integrated Commissioning overspend of £6.935m driven by demand growth that the council expects to continue into 2026-27
findings.detail: Adults, Ageing & Wellbeing's Integrated Commissioning service overspent significantly, with care commitments exceeding budget by £2.078m at year start and further pressure from 276 packages costing over £100k annually (up 27 from prior year). The council explicitly states: "the scale of existing commitments and the ongoing demand growth are expected to continue to place significant pressure on the Integrated Commissioning budget during financial year 2026-27."
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether demand-driven pressures in the council's largest social care budget are being managed or are structural problems. An explicit forward-warning of continuing pressure suggests the latter.
findings.figures: £6.935m overspend; 276 packages over £100k (up 27); average cost £0.174m per learning disability client
findings.quote: the scale of existing commitments and the ongoing demand growth are expected to continue to place significant pressure on the Integrated Commissioning budget during financial year 2026-27

findings.headline: Proposed fees and charges increases for home-to-school transport and adult social care require consultation with undefined fallback plan
findings.detail: Council has identified proposals to raise income through fees and charges, 'including some proposals relating to home to school transport and some charges for adult social care, which could be achieved by combining a number of different changes to charging policies'. These 'will be subject to consultation because they reflect changes in the underlying charging policy as opposed to revised estimates of costs'. Critically: 'In the event that following consultation the proposed level of savings cannot be achieved, alternative compensating savings will be brought forward.' These compensating savings are not identified.
findings.matters: Unspecified 'alternative compensating savings' are a placeholder for undefined budget cuts, suggesting the council may have exhausted implementable efficiency options and is relying on options that may be politically or operationally unachievable.
findings.figures: Specific fee increase amounts not yet determined (subject to spring 2026 consultation); impact includes home-to-school transport and adult social care charges
findings.quote: These include some proposals relating to home to school transport and some charges for adult social care, which could be achieved by combining a number of different changes to charging policies. A detailed consultation will be issued in the spring setting out a full range of options for achieving these savings. In the event that following consultation the proposed level of savings cannot be achieved, alternative compensating savings will be brought forward.

findings.headline: Despite 2% adult social care precept, council notes 'significant recurrent on-going pressure' in ASC funding
findings.detail: Council is implementing the maximum 2.00% Adult Social Care precept allowed (raising £5.7m), applied across all three years of MTFP. However, the report explicitly states: 'there remains a significant recurrent on-going pressure which needs to be funded by the Council' in Adult Social Care. This means precept income plus ASC grant are insufficient to meet demographic demand for social care.
findings.matters: Acknowledging unmet ASC funding needs despite maximum precept increases signals either service rationing, unmet need, or cross-subsidy from other council budgets—all indicate unsustainable care provision and demographic pressures exceeding available funding.
findings.figures: 2.00% precept increase raising £5.700m recurrent; applied to all three MTFP years; ASC remains under-resourced despite maximum uplift
findings.quote: In addition to the grants mentioned earlier, the increase of 2.00% Adult Social Care Precept to Council Tax levels for 2026-27, and 2.00% thereafter over the remaining duration of the MTFP has provided some additional funding to meet the increasing costs of Adult Social Care. However, there remains a significant recurrent on-going pressure which needs to be funded by the Council.

findings.headline: Business Rates revaluation increased asset value by 17% but multiplier adjustments stripped all benefit
findings.detail: Business Rates properties revalued for 2026-27, increasing Northumberland's rateable value from £262.047m to £307.321m (£45.274m increase, 17.3% growth). However, 'the Council will not benefit from the revaluation increase, as adjustments have been made to the Business Rates multipliers in an equal and opposite way to offset the impact of the increased valuation making it revenue neutral for each local authority'. Only true growth above the Baseline Funding Level (BFL) benefits councils. This is not revenue neutral in practice—it reduces the council's ability to grow rates income through asset revaluation.
findings.matters: A major asset revaluation yielded zero funding benefit, illustrating how centrally-controlled multiplier adjustments neutralise local tax base improvements and limit council revenue growth.
findings.figures: Rateable value increased £262.047m → £307.321m (£45.274m growth); net benefit to council £0
findings.quote: For the financial year 2026-27 all Business Rates properties have been revalued. The outcome of the exercise increased the Council's rateable value from the 2023 list value of £262.047 million to £307.321 million on the 2026 list... However, the Council will not benefit from the revaluation increase, as adjustments have been made to the Business Rates multipliers in an equal and opposite way to offset the impact of the increased valuation making it revenue neutral for each local authority.

findings.headline: Council will draw down net £27.4m from Strategic Management Reserve over MTFP to balance budget
findings.detail: Proposed net contributions of £18.777m (2026-27), £12.582m (2027-28) from the Strategic Management Reserve, then £3.932m contribution back in 2028-29. This £27.427m draw is intended to bring general reserves back within the target 5.0-7.5% range. Using reserves to bridge annual budget gaps indicates the council is managing a structural deficit, not a cyclical pressure. Current reserve level will 'exceed £77.236 million' at 31 March 2026, but planned drawdowns are essential to the budget.
findings.matters: Reserves are being used to fund ongoing operations rather than one-off items. This pattern signals the council cannot cover its recurrent spending from recurrent income, reducing financial resilience and the ability to respond to unexpected costs.
findings.figures: Net drawdown of £27.427m over MTFP; general reserves target 5.0-7.5% of gross budget (£51.491m-£77.236m for 2026-27)
findings.quote: It is proposed to utilise a net contribution of £27.427 million from the Strategic Management Reserve over the duration of the MTFP 2026-29, comprising of net contributions from the Strategic Management Reserve of £18.777 million in 2026-27, and £12.582 million in 2027-28, and a net contribution to the Strategic Management Reserve of £3.932 million in 2028-29.

findings.headline: Council requires £18.5m savings in 2026-27 with 'significant reliance on BEST efficiencies' that remain unspecified
findings.detail: The budget requires £18.539m efficiency savings in 2026-27 and £34.631m over 2027-29. The council explicitly states 'significant reliance on BEST efficiencies to balance the budget', but BEST is not defined in the document. Proposals subject to risk: fees and charges increases are 'subject to consultation' with a fallback clause stating 'alternative compensating savings will be brought forward' if the proposed level cannot be achieved.
findings.matters: Reliance on unspecified efficiency programmes creates delivery risk. The fallback to unidentified compensating savings suggests the council may have exhausted visible options, indicating budget-setting on assumptions rather than firm plans.
findings.quote: There is a requirement to deliver efficiencies equating to £18.539 million in 2026-27 and £34.631 million over the remaining two years of the MTFP... note the significant reliance on BEST efficiencies to balance the budget. In the event that following consultation the proposed level of savings cannot be achieved, alternative compensating savings will be brought forward.

findings.headline: Advance Northumberland restructuring costs of £1.5-2.0m per year to be funded from reserves
findings.detail: The council is providing £1.500m (2026-27), £1.740m (2027-28), and £1.990m (2028-29) to cover 'estimated net costs relating to the financial restructuring of Advance Northumberland'. These costs are funded from the Strategic Management Reserve initially. The council states costs 'will be repaid to the Strategic Management Reserve in 2029-30 (year five of Advance Northumberland's Business Plan), as agreed by Council in March 2025', making it 'cost neutral to the Council'—but repayment depends on the company's future profitability.
findings.matters: A council-owned company requiring ongoing subsidy signals either operational difficulties or loan arrangements. The repayment depends on company performance in year 5, creating a contingent liability if the business plan fails.
findings.quote: estimated net costs relating to the financial restructuring of Advance Northumberland of £1.500 million in 2026-27, £1.740 million in 2027-28, and £1.990 million in 2028-29... These costs will be repaid to the Strategic Management Reserve in 2029-30 (year five of Advance Northumberland's Business Plan), as agreed by Council in March 2025 and are therefore cost neutral to the Council.

findings.headline: Special educational needs deficits forecast to grow from £15.4m to £21.7m in one year
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant reserve shows a deficit of £15.414 million at 31 March 2026, driven by rising pupils with EHCPs requiring place funding and top-ups. In 2026-27 this worsens to £21.673 million if growth continues. The council explicitly warns this 'could result in the Council needing to borrow more money than anticipated to meet its cash requirements. The borrowing will in turn result in an increased cost of borrowing.'
findings.matters: Growing education deficits reduce financial flexibility and force unplanned borrowing, directly increasing debt costs. This signals rising demand the council cannot fund from sustainable sources.
findings.figures: £15.414m deficit at 31 March 2026 → £21.673m forecast by end of 2026-27; in-year overspend on High Needs Block of £7.994m in 2025-26
findings.quote: The overall DSG unusable reserve is forecast to show a deficit of £15.414 million at the end of the 2025-26 financial year... In 2026-27 the overall DSG unusable reserve is expected to move to a deficit of £21.673 million if growth continues at the current rate... The rising deficit will have an impact on the Council's cashflow which if it continues to grow significantly, could result in the Council needing to borrow more money than anticipated to meet its cash requirements.

findings.paper_title: Appointment of Executive Director of Transformation and Resources - s151 Officer - corrected
findings.headline: S151 Officer transition: incumbent departing 28 February, replacement starting 1 May 2026 with interim acting-up period
findings.detail: Jan Willis, Executive Director of Finance (S151 Officer), will leave employment on 28 February 2026. Jon Ritchie is appointed to take post on 1 May 2026. Alison Elsdon, Director of Finance and Procurement (Deputy s151 Officer) will act up from 1 March until Mr Ritchie's start date. Ritchie is a member of ICAEW and was selected following comprehensive recruitment process and assessment centre evaluation.
findings.matters: The s151 Officer is the statutory chief finance officer responsible for the council's financial administration; lenders track transitions in this key role to ensure continuity of financial governance, particularly where there is a gap between the outgoing and incoming permanent appointments.
findings.figures: Willis departure: 28 February 2026. Interim acting-up period: 1 March to 1 May 2026 (two months). Ritchie start: 1 May 2026. Salary: £165,728 per annum.
findings.quote: Jan Willis, Executive Director of Finance (S151 Officer), will leave employment on 28 February 2026. It is proposed that Alison Elsdon, Director of Finance and Procurement (Deputy s151 Officer) act up for the period from 1 March 2026 until Mr Ritchie's start date.

findings.headline: 2027-28 budget gap of £3.257 million identified; further work needed for years 2 and 3 of MTFP
findings.detail: Even with the indicative government grant figures for the three-year settlement period (2026-27 to 2028-29), the council identified a budget gap of £3.257 million for 2027-28. The document states "Further work is needed for years 2027-28 and 2028-29 to identify additional efficiencies in light of further potential pressures or items of growth beyond those already built into the MTFP." The S151 Officer notes sustained focus on a balanced budget over the medium term is essential.
findings.matters: The council has not yet identified solutions for the 2027-28 budget gap. This is being bridged temporarily by a Strategic Management Reserve contribution, but reflects uncertainty about future funding and the sufficiency of the savings programme.
findings.figures: Budget gap 2027-28: £3.257 million
findings.quote: This left a budget gap of £3.257 million for 2027-28 but a forecast surplus for 2028-29. In order to smooth these year-on-year movements a contribution from the Strategic Management Reserve to this value will be made in 2027-28 and repaid from the surplus in 2028-29. Further work is needed for years 2027-28 and 2028-29 to identify additional efficiencies in light of further potential pressures or items of growth beyond those already built into the MTFP.

findings.headline: Adult social care demand growth forecast to impose additional £7.077 million cost risk over MTFP if above assumptions
findings.detail: The budget includes growth for demographic and demand pressures in adult social care from 2026-27 onwards. The council estimates that a continued increase in demand above assumed levels could result in additional costs of £7.077 million over the MTFP. This sits alongside the immediate pressure in children's social care and is not separately itemized in headline savings targets.
findings.matters: Adult social care is demand-led and ageing demographics are structural. The council's assumption may be conservative; if actual demand exceeds forecast by even a small percentage, it will require either service reductions or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: Potential additional cost over MTFP if adult social care demand exceeds forecast: £7.077 million
findings.quote: In adult social care, growth has been built in for demographic demand pressures from 2026-27 onwards. A continued increase in demand above the assumed level of growth could result in additional costs over the life of the MTFP of £7.077 million based on projections.

findings.headline: CIPFA Resilience Index flags high risk on interest payable and gross external debt despite low reserves risk
findings.detail: The council's 2024-25 CIPFA Resilience Index shows low risk for four of eight primary indicators (including reserves), but high risk for Interest Payable as % of Net Revenue Expenditure and Gross External Debt. The high debt is driven by lending to Advance Northumberland and other entities (£389.760 million at March 2025), which inflates both debt and interest costs. The index does not account for repayment status or security held.
findings.matters: While the S151 Officer argues the index understates the council's position by excluding interest receivable and security held, the underlying fact remains: the council carries material third-party debt that generates significant annual interest costs, constraining financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Lending to third parties (March 2025): £389.760 million; CIPFA Resilience Index: high risk on two of eight primary indicators; all existing debt at fixed rates
findings.quote: For Northumberland, the two indicators are inextricably linked. Members will be aware that the Council's debt has historically been at a high level due to the level of lending to other organisations such as Advance Northumberland and its predecessor Arch, and Northumbria Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust (at 31 March 2025 the Council lending to third parties was £389.760 million)

findings.headline: Advance Northumberland restructuring requires £3.730 million funding over MTFP; dependent on company repayment
findings.detail: The council is restructuring debt for Advance Northumberland (property/housing company) to secure long-term sustainability. The council estimates a net cost of £1.500 million in 2026-27 and £3.730 million over the MTFP. The plan depends on Advance Northumberland repaying this from its business plan and thereafter paying an annual dividend. This is funded from Strategic Management Reserve and requires close monitoring.
findings.matters: The council holds £389.760 million of lending to third parties as at March 2025, with Advance Northumberland as a key exposure. The restructuring is necessary but represents additional near-term cost dependent on the company's operational recovery. If the company fails to repay, it becomes a permanent reserve drain.
findings.figures: Net cost 2026-27: £1.500 million; total MTFP cost: £3.730 million; council lending to third parties (March 2025): £389.760 million
findings.quote: The Council's Budget 2026-27 and MTFP 2026-2029 contains the best estimate of the net cost to the Council of the restructuring. The 2026-27 Budget contains a net cost of £1.500 million and costs totalling £3.730 million are included over the remaining duration of the MTFP. These costs will initially be funded from the Strategic Management Reserve, and this is factored into the figures shown in the Budget 2026-27 and MTFP 2026-2029. It is anticipated that AN will repay this sum to the Council by the end of its current 5-year Business Plan which will enable the Strategic Management Reserve to be replenished.

findings.headline: Council tax collection rate declining: 99.25% (2020-21) to 97.24% (2024-25); 1% further decline would add £5.855 million to budget gap
findings.detail: Council tax collection rates have eroded from 99.25% in 2020-21 to 97.24% in 2024-25, a cumulative loss of 2.01 percentage points. The collection rate year-to-date for 2025-26 is 80.65%, though staff continue to collect for prior years. The council assumes 99% collection rate in budget, but notes that a 1% reduction in the assumed collection rate would add £5.855 million to the budget gap over the MTFP.
findings.matters: Declining collection rates suggest households and businesses are under financial stress. The 2pp decline already achieved means budget assumptions may be optimistic, and further erosion would force additional savings or service reductions.
findings.figures: Collection rates: 2020-21 99.25%, 2024-25 97.24%, 2025-26 YTD 80.65%; sensitivity: 1% reduction in collection rate = £5.855 million budget impact over MTFP
findings.quote: A reduction in the assumed growth in the Council Tax base of 25% would add £1.458 million to the budget gap over the life of the MTFP and a 1% reduction in the collection rate would add a further £5.855 million.

findings.headline: Strategic Management Reserve being drawn down to balance 2026-27 budget; further drawdown needed for 2027-28
findings.detail: The council is using the Strategic Management Reserve to fund £18.777 million of non-recurrent items in 2026-27 to achieve a balanced budget (alongside £18.539 million of savings and 4.99% council tax increase). A further contribution from the Strategic Management Reserve is planned for 2027-28 to cover a £3.257 million budget gap, to be repaid from the forecast surplus in 2028-29.
findings.matters: Relying on reserve drawdown to balance the budget, particularly over multiple years, indicates the council cannot fund its base operations from recurring revenue. The 2027-28 gap requires further detailed work, and the 2028-29 repayment depends on achieving a forecast surplus.
findings.figures: Strategic Management Reserve used for £18.777 million non-recurrent costs in 2026-27; £3.257 million contribution planned for 2027-28; General Fund balance currently £51.310 million
findings.quote: The Strategic Management Reserve will be used to fund non-recurrent items of expenditure totalling £18.777 million... In order to show a balanced budget over the 3 years of the MTFP, the indicative figures provided by the Government in the provisional settlement are shown. This left a budget gap of £3.257 million for 2027-28 but a forecast surplus for 2028-29.

findings.headline: Large savings programme (£53.170 million over MTFP) required; future-year deliverability has lower confidence than 2026-27
findings.detail: The council must deliver £53.170 million of savings over the three-year MTFP to balance the budget, including £18.539 million in 2026-27. The BEST programme is the primary vehicle, with £42.336 million of recurrent savings built in. Whilst 2025-26 savings are tracking at 87% green/amber, the document notes "more confidence about deliverability in year 1 than in later years" and states "Failure to deliver these savings would inevitably require deep cuts to front line services."
findings.matters: The council's balanced budget is contingent on delivery of savings with explicitly acknowledged diminishing confidence in years 2 and 3. This creates downside risk if transformation slips or if savings prove unachievable without service reductions.
findings.figures: Total savings required: £53.170 million over MTFP; 2026-27: £18.539 million; BEST programme: £42.336 million recurrent over MTFP
findings.quote: Recurrent savings of £42.336 million over the years 2026-27 to 2028-29 have been built into the MTFP for the BEST programme... Whilst plans are in place to deliver some of these savings, with more confidence about deliverability in year 1 than in later years, there needs to be an appropriate level of organisational focus in order to deliver the revenue savings that are currently planned which make a substantial contribution to closing the budget gap in the MTFP. Failure to deliver these savings would inevitably require deep cuts to front line services.

findings.headline: Capital programme financing ratio rising unsustainably: from 13.6% (2025-26) to 19.6% (2028-29)
findings.detail: The Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream—the primary prudential indicator of capital affordability—is forecast to rise from 13.6% in 2025-26 to 18.2% in 2026-27 and 19.6% by 2028-29 (General Fund). Using the council's preferred local indicator that includes interest receivable, the ratio is 14.1% in 2026-27 rising to 15.4% in 2028-29. The S151 Officer explicitly states this level of increase is not sustainable.
findings.matters: The council acknowledges its capital programme is on an unsustainable financing trajectory. This signals that either capital expenditure must be capped or new funding sources (grants, capital receipts) must be identified, both of which constrain service delivery capacity.
findings.figures: Ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream: 2025-26 13.6%, 2026-27 18.2% (or 14.1% with interest receivable), 2028-29 19.6% (or 15.4%)
findings.quote: This level of increase is not sustainable in the long term and consideration will need to be given to capping financing costs going forward in order to ensure that the capital programme remains affordable within the context of the Council's overall financial resources and budgetary pressures.

findings.headline: Schools reserves at risk: 25 schools currently in deficit; worst-case scenario projects 49 schools in deficit by 2028
findings.detail: Schools are accumulating deficits across the authority. Currently 25 schools hold deficits ranging from £0.003 million to £1.916 million (the largest is a special school). The worst-case forecast shows 49 schools in deficit by 31 March 2028, with some exceeding £3.7 million. Accumulated deficits for schools issued academy orders are borne by the council and call on general reserves.
findings.matters: School deficits represent a diffuse but growing contingent liability. The projection to 49 schools in deficit suggests systemic pressure in the school funding model that the High Needs Block transfer alone (£1.273 million) does not address.
findings.figures: 25 schools in deficit currently; largest deficit £1.916 million (special school); worst case 49 schools in deficit by 31 March 2028 with deficits up to £3.742 million
findings.quote: There are currently 25 schools in deficit with deficits ranging from £0.003 million to £1.916 million. The school with the largest deficit is a special school and there is a rapid review underway of the funding model and the wider use of the High Needs Block to support all students with special educational needs across the County. The worst-case scenario anticipates that 49 schools will be in deficit by 31 March 2028 with deficits ranging from £0.004 million to £3.742 million.

findings.headline: High Needs Block (SEND) deficit forecast to reach £22.164 million in 2026-27, up from £15.899 million at 2025-26 year-end
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit is growing rapidly, driven by in-year overspend of £8.487 million on the High Needs Block due to increased place funding and top-up costs for pupils with Education, Health and Care Plans. The council receives a one-off 90% grant covering the deficit at end of 2025-26 (£14.310 million estimated), but must fund 10% (£1.590 million in 2025-26; £0.626 million in 2026-27; £0.801 million in 2027-28). Deficits are expected to continue accumulating in 2026-27 and 2027-28 with no clear resolution.
findings.matters: The deficit is held in an unusable reserve but represents a contingent liability if the statutory override ends without government intervention. Future SEND reform timing and scope remain uncertain, creating unquantified risk beyond 2028.
findings.figures: DSG deficit £15.899 million forecast end 2025-26, rising to £22.164 million in 2026-27; in-year overspend £8.487 million; High Needs Stability Grant £14.310 million (90%) announced; council to fund remaining 10%
findings.quote: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit, which is expected to be £15.899 million at the end of the 2025-26 financial year, rising to £22.164 million in 2026-27 represents a growing risk to the Council's financial standing. The deficit includes an in year overspend on the high needs block (SEND) of £8.487 million due to increased place funding and top-up costs associated with rising numbers of pupils with an Education, Health and Care Plan.

findings.headline: Children in care caseload surged from 456 to 543 in a single financial year, driving external placement costs
findings.detail: The number of children in care rose sharply from 456 at March 2025 to 543 currently, with external residential placements increasing from 79 to 84. The council has added £7.441 million of recurrent budget growth for Children's Social Care in 2026-27 (total including other pressures: £9.120 million). Each additional external placement above assumed growth adds £0.345 million annually.
findings.matters: The scale and speed of demand growth (19% increase in 12 months) suggests demographic or systemic shifts beyond the council's control. This directly impacts borrowing affordability and sets a trajectory for sustained budget pressure.
findings.figures: Children in care up from 456 to 543; external placements 79 to 84; budget growth of £7.441 million for 2026-27; each additional placement costs £0.345 million annually
findings.quote: During 2025-26 the number children cared for has risen from 456 at the end of March 2025 to 543 (current), placing significant pressure on the external residential placements budget. This has meant that more children have been cared for within external homes and at a distance (an increase from 79 to 84 during the financial year).

findings.headline: Current 2025-26 financial year showing mid-year overspend of £3.334 million driven by social care demand
findings.detail: The council identified significant demand pressures in adults and children's social care during 2025-26, resulting in a mid-year forecast services overspend of £3.334 million (net of corporate items). This emerged despite 87% of planned 2025-26 savings on track. The council has implemented weekly Spend Control Boards and expanded the Vacancy Panel to manage the shortfall.
findings.matters: Active overspend in the current financial year signals that demand management is outpacing control measures, and the council is drawing on reserves to manage it. This questions whether planned savings programmes will suffice going forward.
findings.figures: £3.334 million mid-year forecast overspend; £10.409 million of £16.299 million savings RAG-rated green
findings.quote: there are significant and rapidly increasing pressures on service budgets arising from demand for adults and children's social care, resulting in a mid-year forecast services overspend of £3.334 million net of corporate items and transfers from reserves and contingencies

findings.paper_title: 07.3.1 S25 Statement Appendix 1 MTFP 2026-29 - Sensitivity Analysis
findings.headline: The council is relying on an 8.5% vacancy factor in Adult Social Care (£44.886m budget); non-achievement would cost £1.347m over three years.
findings.detail: The sensitivity analysis models the risk that Adult Social Care vacancies do not materialise. The base budget assumes an 8.5% vacancy factor on a £44.886m staff budget. If vacancies close faster than expected or recruitment is stronger than planned, the council faces a £0.449m annual pressure.
findings.matters: Over-reliance on vacancy factors to balance the budget is a known risk; stronger-than-expected recruitment or vacancy closure creates unbudgeted payroll pressure that the council has no contingency to absorb.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care budget: £44.886m; vacancy factor: 8.50%; cost of non-achievement: £0.449m per year (£1.347m over 3 years)
findings.quote: Non Achievement of Adults Vacancy Factor ... Current vacancy factor is 8.50% of the Adult Social Care staff budget of £44.886 million

findings.paper_title: 07.3.1 S25 Statement Appendix 1 MTFP 2026-29 - Sensitivity Analysis
findings.headline: A 1% rise in interest rates would cost £2.332m to £3.143m per year, totalling £6.363m over the MTFP, based on the capital programme.
findings.detail: The sensitivity analysis models interest rate exposure across the capital programme. A 1% rate change creates a £2.332m impact in 2026-27, peaking at £3.143m in 2027-28 before declining to £0.888m in 2028-29, reflecting the profile of borrowing over the period.
findings.matters: Material interest rate exposure means debt service costs could rise significantly if rates increase; the council has limited ability to absorb this without further service reductions or reserve drawdown.
findings.quote: Change in Interest Rates ... Change by 1.00%. Impact on the net cost of capital based on the Capital Programme within the 2026-29 MTFP

findings.paper_title: 07.3.1 S25 Statement Appendix 1 MTFP 2026-29 - Sensitivity Analysis
findings.headline: The council models a 10% efficiency savings non-delivery risk worth £1.854m to £1.664m per year (total £5.317m).
findings.detail: The sensitivity analysis explicitly recognises that efficiency savings carry delivery risk. The 'Efficiencies (non-delivery)' line assumes 10% of planned savings—including Best initiatives and 10% of savings not yet identified—will not materialise, costing £1.854m in 2026-27, £1.799m in 2027-28, and £1.664m in 2028-29.
findings.matters: The council acknowledges material downside risk on its savings programme; if efficiencies underdeliver by more than 10%, or if savings are not yet identified, the budget gap widens significantly.
findings.quote: Efficiencies (non-delivery) ... Potential of non-delivery - 10.00%. Including Best initiatives. plus 10.00% of any savings not yet identified

findings.paper_title: 07.3.1 S25 Statement Appendix 1 MTFP 2026-29 - Sensitivity Analysis
findings.headline: SEN home-to-school transport is modelled for an additional 8% pupil growth above already-agreed increases, representing 134–156 extra pupils over the MTFP.
findings.detail: The sensitivity analysis assumes an 8% additional growth in SEN transport pupil numbers in each year beyond the growth already in the base budget. This translates to 134 additional pupils in 2026-27, 144 in 2027-28, and 156 in 2028-29, creating a cumulative pressure of £1.762m.
findings.matters: Sustained SEN demand growth that exceeds planning assumptions creates recurrent budget pressure without identified funding; the council may face difficult choices if this trend materialises.
findings.quote: Based on a further 8.00% change in pupil numbers over and above the growth already agreed split through the year. This is equivalent to 134 pupils above anticipated growth in SEN Transport.

findings.paper_title: 07.3.1 S25 Statement Appendix 1 MTFP 2026-29 - Sensitivity Analysis
findings.headline: Adult social care demand carries £6.0m to £7.077m upside risk over three years based on demographic trend analysis and ONS population projections.
findings.detail: The sensitivity analysis models adult social care demand using 3-year trend analysis of learning disability independent supported living growth and ONS population projections. Upside risks range from £2.0m to £2.359m per year across the three years.
findings.matters: Persistent adult social care demand growth suggests the council may struggle to contain costs in its largest budget area; failure to manage this creates material reserve depletion risk.
findings.quote: The budget increase is the potential additional pressure based on a 3 year trend analysis of service growth in learning disability independent supported living settings, and Office for National Statistics population projections to estimate future demand for older people's services.

findings.paper_title: 07.3.1 S25 Statement Appendix 1 MTFP 2026-29 - Sensitivity Analysis
findings.headline: Children's external residential placements are projected to create a recurrent £1.723m annual pressure based on 5 additional placements.
findings.detail: The sensitivity analysis budgets for 5 additional external residential placements for children at an average cost of £6,629 per week. This creates a £1.723m recurring pressure in each year of the MTFP, totalling £5.169m over three years.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted growth in high-cost placements signals rising complexity in children's caseloads; if this trend continues above the 5-placement assumption, it creates unplanned overspend risk.
findings.figures: 5 placements × £6,629 per week = £1.723m per year; £5.169m over 3 years
findings.quote: Significant Cost Increase for Additional External Residential Placements for Children ... Based on 5 placements at an average cost of £6,629 per week

findings.headline: Energy efficiency funding bid fell short: applied for £7.508m but received £3.533m (47% of requested grant)
findings.detail: The council applied for £7.508m from the Warm Homes: Social Housing Fund Wave 3 scheme (with a matching HRA contribution) but the final grant award was only £3.533m with an equal HRA contribution. The scheme involves upgrading social housing stock to Energy Performance Certificate band C standard.
findings.matters: A significant gap between the requested and awarded external funding (53% shortfall) indicates either the bid was over-optimistic or the programme is less competitive than anticipated. The reduced grant means either fewer homes will be upgraded or the HRA must make a larger contribution than originally planned.
findings.figures: Bid requested: £7.508m; final award: £3.533m; HRA contribution also £3.533m
findings.quote: Cabinet agreed on 12 November 2024 to submit an application for funding from the Warm Homes: Social Housing Fund Wave 3 to implement energy efficiency measures into the Council's social housing. The initial bid was for a three-year investment of £7.508 million, with HRA contribution of £7.000 million, however the final grant award was £3.533 million with HRA contribution of £3.533 million.

findings.headline: Non-traditional housing stock in portfolio requires significant investment or intervention with no quantified plan
findings.detail: The council acknowledges it holds "a number of non-traditional homes that will require significant investment or intervention" as part of broader emerging investment needs linked to the structure and age of properties. This is listed as a current priority but with no specific budget allocation or timeline provided.
findings.matters: Non-traditional housing is known to present cost and liability challenges across the social housing sector. The council's admission that significant intervention is needed but absence of a costed plan indicates emerging liability that could generate future budget shocks.
findings.figures: No figures quantified
findings.quote: Northumberland holds a number of non-traditional homes that will require significant investment or intervention.

findings.headline: Windmill Grove development (31 properties, £9.766m) is not yet funded and not reflected in the MTFP
findings.detail: The council is planning a major mixed-tenure development of 31 properties at Windmill Grove with an overall cost of approximately £9.766m, including demolition and site fees. Demolition is planned for February-April 2026 with site start expected late 2026. However, the scheme "and its budget are not reflected in this MTFP as work is currently taking place to review different funding streams."
findings.matters: A £9.7m capital scheme starting within months but without identified funding or budget provision signals either overoptimism about external funding or a lack of capital planning discipline. The absence from the MTFP means the council cannot yet demonstrate how this will be funded without further reserve depletion or borrowing.
findings.figures: Total cost approximately £9.766m; not included in MTFP; demolition Feb-Apr 2026, site start late 2026
findings.quote: The overall cost of the development will be approximately £9.766 million, which includes the demolition and takes into consideration all potential fees and risks associated with Brownfield land. This scheme and its budget are not reflected in this MTFP as work is currently taking place to review different funding streams.

findings.headline: Specific major repairs with fire safety implications: Beaumont Street flats fire compartmentation defects (£1.25m)
findings.detail: The 2026-27 capital programme includes £1.25m to address fire compartmentation defects at Beaumont Street flats following a fire in 2023. This is part of a broader pattern of reactive capital works driven by specific incidents or hazards rather than planned maintenance.
findings.matters: Fire safety remediation is a statutory and urgent matter. The significant cost to address defects from a 2023 incident indicates the council may have deferred compliance work or been slow to act on identified hazards. This pattern of reactive spending competes with planned capital investment.
findings.figures: £1.25m for Beaumont Street flats; also £0.5m for Allensgreen homes post-fire, £0.16m for Augur Place damp remediation
findings.quote: Work to the fabric of Beaumont Street flats to bring homes back into use and address fire compartmentation defects that that were identified following a fire in 2023 - £1.250 million

findings.headline: Stock condition survey backlog: last survey of only 10% of homes was in 2012; council rushing to catch up by March 2027
findings.detail: The council is allocating £1.4m to commission external consultants to complete a full stock condition survey by 31 March 2027. The last survey was conducted in 2012 on only 10% of homes. The council notes this exercise "will generate additional works and put further pressure on the reactive maintenance and repairs team" and "may also identify improvement works that are required to be added to the capital programme going forward."
findings.matters: A 14-year-old survey covering only 10% of stock means the council's understanding of its asset condition is severely outdated. The acknowledged likelihood that the survey will identify significant new works signals potential hidden capital liabilities not yet reflected in budgets or reserves.
findings.figures: £1.4m for external consultant surveys to be completed by 31 March 2027; last survey 2012 on 10% of stock
findings.quote: The last stock condition survey exercise was carried out on 10% of council-owned homes in 2012... It is anticipated that this exercise will generate additional works and put further pressure on the reactive maintenance and repairs team. It may also identify improvement works that are required to be added to the capital programme going forward.

findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing inspection found health and safety data discrepancies requiring system implementation
findings.detail: The council notes that a recent inspection by the Regulator of Social Housing "has highlighted discrepancies in health and safety data." Although the council states it is confident statutory responsibilities are being met, it acknowledges the need to implement a compliance system that is "fit for purpose" and allocate resources for effective implementation and ongoing accuracy monitoring.
findings.matters: Data discrepancies flagged by the regulator indicate a control weakness in the organisation's compliance infrastructure. This is a governance issue that could escalate to intervention if not resolved. Implementation of remedial systems will require sustained investment.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this budget; flagged as an emerging priority
findings.quote: The recent inspection carried out on the Housing Service by the Regulator of Social Housing has highlighted discrepancies in health and safety data. Whilst the Council is confident that statutory health and safety responsibilities as a landlord are being met, there is a need to ensure effective capturing, monitoring, and reporting on all health and safety workstreams. The current software does not do this therefore the purchase and implementation of a compliance system that is fit for purpose should be considered.

findings.headline: Borrowing costs have doubled in five years and are forecast to remain above 4% through 2029-30
findings.detail: Interest rates for HRA borrowing have risen from an average of 2.00% in 2021-22 to an estimated 5.31% in 2026-27. Despite expectations that rates would fall more rapidly, inflation picked up during 2025-26, slowing the anticipated reduction. Borrowing costs are now forecast to remain above 4.00% until 2029-30.
findings.matters: High sustained borrowing costs constrain a council's capital spending power and revenue capacity. A lender assessing refinancing risk or credit standing needs to know whether the council can service debt comfortably under this cost regime.
findings.quote: interest rates for borrowing have risen significantly, increasing from an average of 2.00% in 2021-22 to an estimated 5.31% in 2026-27. Although rates were initially expected to fall more rapidly during 2025-26 as inflation eased, inflation picked up again during the year, slowing the anticipated reduction. As a result, borrowing costs are now forecast to remain above 4.00% until 2029-30.

findings.headline: HRA reserves declining to near-minimum level with acknowledged overspend risk
findings.detail: The HRA reserve falls from £21.996m (March 2026) to £14.021m (March 2027) and to £13.909m by March 2030. The council explicitly states that an overspend between 2026-27 and 2029-30 could breach the £10.0m minimum reserve level agreed with the Regulator. The plan depletes reserves to fund the capital programme while interest rates remain high, leaving limited headroom.
findings.matters: A council approaching its minimum reserve floor signals financial stress and constrains flexibility for new pressures or opportunities. The acknowledged risk of breaching the limit is a leading indicator of potential intervention.
findings.figures: Reserve balance £21.996m → £14.021m → £13.909m; minimum agreed level £10.0m
findings.quote: There is a risk that if there is an overspend between 2026-27 and 2029-30 that this could take the reserves under the agreed reserves limit of £10.000 million, therefore will need to be monitored carefully during the year.

findings.headline: General Fund borrowing requirement of £330.8m over three years, averaging £110.3m annually for first two years
findings.detail: The council plans General Fund borrowing of £144.4m (2026-27), £124.8m (2027-28), and £61.6m (2028-29) to finance capital projects. Combined with HRA contributions of £46.7m, total capital financing from internal borrowing/reserves is £377.5m.
findings.matters: This scale of planned borrowing directly impacts the council's debt service costs in future years and must be evaluated against revenue-raising capacity to service the debt.

findings.headline: Capital receipts from asset sales fall 70% from £19.8m to £6.0m, indicating depleting sale capacity
findings.detail: Planned capital receipts decline from £19.8m in 2026-27 to £12.5m in 2027-28 and £6.0m in 2028-29. This steep decline in this funding source reduces the council's flexibility for future capital programmes.
findings.matters: Falling receipts indicate limited remaining opportunity for asset disposals and signal constraints on the council's ability to fund capital programmes from non-borrowing sources.

findings.headline: Capital programme contracts to £165.2m in 2028-29, a 51% decline from £340.5m in 2026-27
findings.detail: The council's planned capital spending halves by the third year of the programme. 2026-27 at £340.5m falls to £300.2m in 2027-28 and £165.2m in 2028-29. This sharp contraction suggests either completion of major programmes or constraints on future capital capacity.
findings.matters: The trajectory signals where the council's capital priorities will be in future years and whether infrastructure investment capacity is constrained by debt or other factors.

findings.headline: Nearly half the capital programme (£377.7m, 46.9%) depends on external grants that appear to be scheme-specific and time-limited
findings.detail: The programme relies on £377.7m in external grants including Borderlands schemes, Levelling Up Funds, CRSTS, and other time-limited initiatives spread across three years. The detailed project listings show individual projects dependent on these grants with no indication of confirmed funding.
findings.matters: If planned external grants do not materialise or are reduced, the council's borrowing requirement increases correspondingly, affecting debt service costs and financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Council is dependent on interest income from loans to third parties to offset borrowing costs.
findings.detail: Northumberland receives significant interest from loans to Advance Northumberland Limited and Northumberland Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust, stated as being in support of service objectives rather than to generate returns. This interest is material: it reduces the financing cost ratio by 4.1 percentage points (from 18.2% to 14.1% in 2026-27). This creates a reliance on investee income to maintain affordability metrics.
findings.matters: The council's stated affordability depends partly on investment income from related entities. If these investments underperform or the arrangements are restructured, the financing cost ratio would rise, worsening financial metrics and potentially signalling affordability stress.
findings.figures: Difference between statutory ratio (18.2% in 2026-27) and local indicator including interest receivable (14.1%) = 4.1 percentage points; income from Commercial and Service Investments averages 3.2-3.7% of net revenue stream across the period
findings.quote: The Council receives significant interest from third parties such as Advance Northumberland Limited and Northumberland Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust. This income is excluded from the statutory indicator above, which shows the ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream. This interest offsets a proportion of the financing costs.

findings.headline: Council is adopting a short-term borrowing strategy due to high interest rates, creating annual refinancing risk.
findings.detail: The Council explicitly states it is borrowing short-term because long-term rates are high. This tactical decision means significant amounts of debt mature each year and must be refinanced. If rates remain elevated or rise further at refinancing dates, costs will increase; if rates fall, the council benefits, but this exposes it to market timing risk.
findings.matters: Short-term borrowing exposes the council to refinancing risk. Large annual maturities mean the council must borrow in the market repeatedly, making it vulnerable to adverse rate movements or market stress.
findings.figures: Maturity limits for 2026-27: under 12 months borrowing capped at 25% (fixed) and 35% (variable); larger limits for longer maturities indicating the maturities can indeed be 'sizeable'
findings.quote: Given that the Council's current borrowing strategy is to borrow short-term due to higher interest rates, the maturities in each year can be sizeable. The contingency is built in so that if the Council needed to borrow in preparation of a loan maturing then the limit won't be breached.

findings.headline: Financing costs consuming an increasing share of General Fund revenue, rising from 13.6% to 19.6% by 2028-29.
findings.detail: The ratio of capital financing costs to net revenue stream is growing sharply. Even after accounting for interest receivable from loans to third parties, the local indicator shows the ratio rising from 8.7% to 15.4%. This means borrowing costs are consuming a growing proportion of the council's discretionary revenue budget.
findings.matters: A rising proportion of revenue going to debt servicing leaves less for service delivery and reduces financial resilience. The 19.6% statutory ratio approaches levels that constrain spending flexibility.
findings.quote: Ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream 2025-26 Estimate 13.6% ... 2028-29 Estimate 19.6%

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increasing by £98.3m over three years, reaching £1,427.8m by 2028-29.
findings.detail: The Council's underlying need to borrow is growing significantly. The CFR (which includes PFI and leasing) rises from £1,257.9m in 2025-26 to £1,427.8m in 2028-29. This represents a long-term commitment to debt servicing that will persist beyond the current planning period.
findings.matters: A growing CFR indicates increasing capital investment is being financed by borrowing, not grants or receipts. This requires sustained revenue provision for debt servicing and limits the council's financial flexibility.
findings.quote: The CFR shown below, which includes other long-term liabilities such as PFI and leasing arrangements, is increasing by £98.318 million over the years 2026-27 to 2028-29

findings.headline: Capital programme contracts 51% from £340.5m to £165.2m by 2028-29
findings.detail: Total capital expenditure falls from £340.504 million in 2026-27 to £165.221 million by 2028-29. This represents a substantial contraction in investment levels, though likely reflects completion of major projects including the Northumberland Line rail service.
findings.matters: A 51% reduction in capital investment signals either successful completion of major infrastructure or potential funding constraints that could affect future service and economic development capacity
findings.quote: Total Capital Expenditure 2025-26 Estimate £m: 332.190, 2026-27 Estimate: 340.504, 2027-28 Estimate: 300.225, 2028-29 Estimate: 165.221

findings.headline: Government policy change allows council to retain 100% of HRA receipts from 2026-27 instead of 48%
findings.detail: Councils previously had to return 52% of Housing Revenue Account capital receipts to government. The Government has now announced 100% retention is allowed indefinitely from 2026-27 onwards, as the Treasury Share will no longer exist.
findings.matters: This increases the council's retained cash from housing asset sales, improving funding flexibility for housing capital investment
findings.figures: From 48% retention to 100% retention from 2026-27
findings.quote: However the Government announced that 100% of HRA capital receipts can be retained by councils indefinitely from 2026-27 onwards as the Treasury Share will no longer exist.

findings.headline: Capital receipts (funding from asset sales) collapse 70% from £19.8m to £6.0m by 2028-29
findings.detail: The council relies on capital receipts to fund capital projects. Receipts are forecast to drop sharply from £19.807 million in 2026-27 to just £5.980 million by 2028-29. The council notes that asset disposal is 'closely monitored', suggesting potential difficulty in achieving these targets.
findings.matters: Declining asset sales reduce funding flexibility for capital investment and may indicate fewer surplus properties available for disposal or challenges in achieving disposal plans
findings.quote: Capital Receipts... 2026-27 Estimate £m: 19.807, 2027-28 Estimate: 12.455, 2028-29 Estimate: 5.980

findings.headline: Council provisions £98.318 million in loans to external bodies including its own economic development company
findings.detail: The capital programme includes £98.318 million over three years for loans to third parties and to Advance Northumberland, the council's wholly-owned economic development company. Loans require financial appraisal and due diligence, with the council seeking security and interest charged to avoid net cost, but this represents significant credit exposure.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand credit exposures the council is taking on and whether default risk could impact the council's financial position
findings.figures: £98.318 million over the three years
findings.quote: The Medium-Term Capital Programme includes a provision of £98.318 million over the three years for loans to third parties.

findings.headline: Investment income declining as interest rates fall, widening the gap between borrowing costs (4.41%) and investment returns (3.40%)
findings.detail: The council forecasts investment returns falling from 4.07% (current) to 3.40% in 2026-27 and remaining at 3.30% in 2027-28 and 2028-29. Simultaneously, new external borrowing is expected to cost 4.41%. This means the council is borrowing at a higher rate than it earns on reserves — a margin that narrows further as investment returns decline.
findings.matters: Declining investment income reduces the council's financial flexibility and makes it harder to fund reserves or service debt from cash generation. The interest rate margin suggests the council is in a cycle of tightening liquidity.
findings.figures: Current investment rate: 4.07%; forecast 2026-27: 3.40%; forecast 2027-28 and 2028-29: 3.30%; new borrowing cost forecast: 4.41%
findings.quote: investment returns are expected to decrease in 2026-27 due to a forecasted decrease in the Bank Rate... Budgeted Rate 3.40% [2026-27]

findings.headline: £289m in outstanding loans to third parties with £98m more planned, heavily concentrated in Advance Northumberland (£187m)
findings.detail: The council has advanced £289m to external entities (64.6% of which is to Advance Northumberland), with plans to lend a further £98.3m. These loans are classified as capital expenditure and sit outside mainstream treasury management, but they represent a material contingent exposure if any borrower defaults or encounters financial difficulty.
findings.matters: Large third-party loans, especially to a single entity like Advance Northumberland, create credit risk concentration. Default or restructuring by a major borrower would hit the council's finances directly. The document states these loans are 'largely only to cover the associated underlying borrowing costs' — implying minimal margin for loss.
findings.figures: Total outstanding third-party loans: £289.156m; Advance Northumberland: £187.015m (64.6% of total); Northumbria Healthcare: £72.460m; planned further advances: £98.318m
findings.quote: Advance Northumberland Group* 187.015 [£m balance]; Estimated Advances to be made: £98.318 million for further loans to Advance Northumberland and other third parties

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing substantially: £101m increase projected for 2026-27 alone
findings.detail: The council's total debt burden (CFR) is rising from £1,170.721m to £1,271.985m in a single year. Over three years to 2028-29, the CFR grows to £1,360.007m — a £189m increase. This sustained growth reflects capital spending outpacing revenue repayment and signals rising long-term debt service commitments.
findings.matters: Growing CFR indicates sustained capital investment (which may be positive) but also rising fixed debt service costs that consume an increasing share of the council's revenue budget over time.
findings.quote: Opening CFR (exc. PFI) 1,170.721 [£m], Increase/(Decrease) in CFR (exc. PFI) 101.264, Closing CFR (exc. PFI) [Need to Borrow] 1,271.985

findings.headline: Material interest rate risk on under-borrowing position if rates remain elevated, with forecasts showing upside risks
findings.detail: The council plans to hold £144m of under-borrowing despite treasury advisors MUFG flagging that 'the overall balance of risks to the forecasts is to the upside' — meaning rates may stay higher than assumed. The council is betting on rates falling to 3.25-3.40% to justify the savings from under-borrowing, but every percentage point above forecast increases the cost of this strategy by ~£1.4m per annum.
findings.matters: If under-borrowing backfires due to rates staying elevated, the council faces unexpected revenue budget pressure, which could force service cuts or require urgent re-borrowing at unfavourable rates.
findings.figures: Under-borrowing: £144.078m; cost of under-borrowing at 3.40% forecast: ~£5.437m per year; forecast new external borrowing rate: 4.41%; notional saving claimed: 1.01% (£1.615m)
findings.quote: The overall balance of risks to the forecasts is to the upside. The impact is that interest rates may be higher than budgeted as the base rate may not fall as forecasted.

findings.headline: £460 million in new external borrowing required in 2026-27 to fund the capital programme
findings.detail: After accounting for £327m in maturing loans, the council plans approximately £460m in fresh external borrowing for 2026-27. The strategy expects this will be met primarily from shorter-term borrowing (up to 2 years), though longer-term borrowing may also be used. This is the largest immediate borrowing need stated in the document.
findings.matters: Lenders need visibility of the council's near-term borrowing requirements and refinancing needs to assess debt service capacity and future market access.
findings.figures: £460 million new external borrowing planned; £327.061 million in maturing loans to be refinanced
findings.quote: a significant amount of new external borrowing will still be required during 2026-27 (estimated at around £460.000 million, after taking into consideration maturing loans of £327.061 million)

findings.headline: Shift from internal borrowing to external borrowing after years of the internal strategy reaching its limit
findings.detail: The council has relied on under-borrowing (using reserves instead of external loans) for years, but that capacity is exhausted. The S151 officer now forecasts 'minimal additional internal borrowing available' and plans to increase external borrowing and reduce the under-borrowing position from £144m. This is a material strategic change in how the council funds its capital programme.
findings.matters: A shift from reserve-funded to debt-funded capital spending signals either rising capital demands or declining reserves, both of which affect a council's future debt servicing capacity and creditworthiness.
findings.figures: Internal borrowing forecast at £144.078m by end of 2026-27 (down from current levels); external borrowing forecast to rise to £1,127.907m from opening £994.968m
findings.quote: since the Council has held this strategy for a number of years, there is minimal additional internal borrowing available and based on the forecast of the Council's resources there will be a need to borrow externally and reduce the internal borrowing position

findings.paper_title: Northumberland CC DRAFT Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Council holds historically high debt to related entities including Advance Northumberland and NHS bodies
findings.detail: The council notes that its debt levels have been 'historically at a high level due to the level of lending to other organisations such as Advance Northumberland and its predecessor Arch and Northumbria Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust'. This creates concentration risk if any borrower faces financial stress.
findings.matters: Lending to related entities (particularly Advance Northumberland, a housing and regeneration company) concentrates credit risk. If borrowers face financial distress, the council could face pressure to write down loans or absorb losses, impacting reserves and financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Amount not quantified in this paper
findings.quote: the Council's debt has historically been at a high level due to the level of lending to other organisations such as Advance Northumberland and its predecessor Arch and Northumbria Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust…as well as being the main source of funding to service the Capital Programme

findings.paper_title: Northumberland CC DRAFT Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: New asset management system migration poses audit-identified risks of misstatement to balance sheet property values
findings.detail: The council is implementing a new asset management system (Civica Property Management) in parallel with the existing system. The auditor explicitly noted 'associated risks of misstatement as a result of the new system', indicating concerns about data integrity, completeness, and valuation during migration.
findings.matters: Property, plant and equipment is material on the balance sheet. Misstatements in asset valuations or completeness could affect financial statement reliability. Dual-running systems create operational complexity and heighten error risk.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: There are associated risks of misstatement as a result of the new system, which is why the Council is implementing the new system in parallel with the existing system

findings.paper_title: Northumberland CC DRAFT Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves have fallen £42.5m (23%) in three years from £183m to £141m
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves declined from £183.148m in 2021/22 to £140.615m in 2024/25, a loss of £42.533m. This erosion reduces the council's financial buffer at precisely the moment when the DSG deficit will require large reserve drawdowns after 2028.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce financial resilience. Combined with the DSG deficit requiring future drawdown and savings delivery shortfalls, this trend signals the council's reserve position could become constrained within the medium term.

findings.paper_title: Northumberland CC DRAFT Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Member Code of Conduct failure: not all members recorded interests; Monitoring Officer considered police referral
findings.detail: The auditor flagged that not all members have recorded sufficient information about conflicts of interest as required by the Code of Conduct. The Monitoring Officer considered whether a police referral was warranted. This governance failure was reported to the Audit and Standards Committee in September 2025, and the auditor will follow up during the 2024/25 audit.
findings.matters: Governance failures around conflicts of interest create reputational and integrity risk. Potential police involvement signals serious misconduct concerns at member level, affecting stakeholder confidence in council decision-making.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: It is a matter of concern to us that, as reported to the Audit and Standards Committee in September, not all Members have met the requirements to record sufficient information and the Monitoring Officer needed to consider whether a referral to the Police was required.

findings.paper_title: Northumberland CC DRAFT Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: First quarter 2025/26 already showing £7.5m overspend despite all-year savings plan
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £7.5m overspend for Q1 2025/26, which represents a material variance in the year's first three months. While the council notes this is typical early-year reporting, it signals that underlying service pressures are high and may require significant corrective action throughout the year.
findings.matters: A £7.5m first-quarter overspend suggests underlying service cost inflation that may not fully resolve within the year, potentially requiring mid-year cuts or late reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £7.5m overspend Q1 2025/26
findings.quote: At quarter one for 2025/26, the Council is reporting an overspend of £7.5 million.

findings.paper_title: Northumberland CC DRAFT Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Savings delivery deteriorating: only 66% achieved in 2024/25 against plan, but 2025/26 target increased to £16.3m
findings.detail: The council planned £10.85m of savings for 2024/25 but only delivered £7.16m, a 34% shortfall. This follows 2023/24 where £1.09m was missed. Despite this track record, savings targets are increasing: £16.299m planned for 2025/26 and £7.834m for 2026/27. This escalation against declining delivery creates significant delivery risk.
findings.matters: Inability to hit savings targets is the leading indicator of budget failure. Higher targets against worsening delivery suggests the council may over-promise and underspend, forcing emergency measures or reserve drawdown mid-year.
findings.figures: 2024/25: planned £10.85m, achieved £7.16m (66% delivery). 2025/26 planned £16.299m. 2026/27 planned £7.834m
findings.quote: Savings of approximately £10.85 million were built into the budget for 2024/2025, not all of which were achieved; however, in the context of the net budget this was not a significant amount.

findings.paper_title: Northumberland CC DRAFT Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit forecast to grow to £43m by 2027-28, when statutory override expires
findings.detail: The council faces a structural problem in SEND spending where costs exceed the ring-fenced grant. The current deficit of £8.053m is forecast to reach £42.999m by 2027-28. The government's statutory override that allows the deficit to be deferred expires on 31 March 2028. Without a funded solution, the council will be forced to finance this from reserves after that date.
findings.matters: This is a material financial risk that will constrain the council's medium-term financial flexibility. Lenders assess councils on reserve sustainability; a £43m deficit hitting reserves in 2028 signals potential borrowing pressure and sharply reduced headroom.
findings.figures: Current deficit £8.053m; forecast 2027-28 £42.999m; forecast 2030-31 £107.593m
findings.quote: The significant and growing deficit is a result of the costs of providing support for special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) exceeding the formula-driven, ring-fenced grant from Government. The time-limited nature of the extension is a financial risk to the Council which requires a long-term solution otherwise the deficit may need to be financed from Council reserves.

findings.headline: 23% of borrowing due within 12 months creates refinancing risk if interest rate forecasts do not materialise.
findings.detail: The council adopted a short-term borrowing strategy (23% due within 12 months, 57% in 10+ years) betting on rate falls from 4.00% to 3.50% by September 2026. If rates remain elevated or fall more slowly, refinancing costs would significantly exceed the current blended rate of 3.41%.
findings.matters: Significant refinancing risk if the council's interest rate forecast proves incorrect, potentially forcing emergency borrowing or further reserve depletion.
findings.figures: 23% of borrowing due within 12 months, blended borrowing rate 3.41%, forecast bank rate falls from 4.00% to 3.50%
findings.quote: The maturity structure of the borrowing shows that a high amount of borrowing is short-term. This is in line with the borrowing strategy to borrow short-term whilst the interest rates are high.

findings.headline: £95.5m in LOBO loans at risk of being called if lenders exercise options in elevated interest rate environment.
